newsitem.title: USA: Military chemical leaks in Baton Rouge suburb.
newsitem.headline: Military chemical leaks in Baton Rouge suburb.

text.p: A container of an irritant used by the U.S. military to train soldiers for chemical warfare was ruptured by a lawn mower in a suburban neighbourhood on Tuesday, injuring a toddler, several firefighters and a paramedic, authorities said.

Fifteen homes in the neighbourhood in an area called Central, just to the north of Baton Rouge, were evacuated for several hours until hazardous materials experts could bag the substance to contain it, police said.
The injured were treated briefly at local hospitals, and the ambulance had to be decontaminated before it could return to service, authorities said.
Authorities would not release the specific location where the incident occurred because they did not want curious people going to the area.

"We know for sure that it was in a vacant lot in this subdivision and that somebody on a bush-hog (lawn mower) hit it this afternoon," said Baton Rouge hazardous materials specialist Benny Hughes. "We know that it affected an 18-month-old baby and a paramedic and the first few volunteer firemen on the scene. But how the stuff got to the lot is kind of murky."

Hughes said the irritant is believed to be CS, a fine yellow powder causing eye and skin irritation like tear gas, that the military uses to train soldiers to deal with chemical warfare. Hughes said CS was simply the name of the chemical and did not stand for its components, which are O-chlorobenzylide malononitrile.

Hughes said the CS was taken from a now-disbanded local Army Reserve unit by a former reservist shortly after the Gulf War. Authorities were not releasing the man's name pending further investigation.
"I don't know if he actually served in Desert Storm but he said he had the stuff in his garage for four or five years and then put it out in the garbage earlier this week."
The former reservist claimed neighbourhood teenagers took the gallon container from his garbage and dumped it in the lot, East Baton Rouge Sheriff's Capt. Paul Maranto said.

But several teens told police the man gave them the chemical, saying they could have some fun with it at parties, Hughes said. "After they opened it and had some problems, they said they threw the container in the lot," he said.
"We're still trying to sort out exactly what that stuff was doing there," East Baton Rouge Parish Sheriff's Capt. Paul Maranto told Reuters.

"A number of state and local charges could be filed later, and the military may want to pursue their own actions, depending on the final analysis of the chemical," he said. "If it was a souvenir, it could turn out to be a very expensive one."
